content.text: Let's talk through the open decisions before you edit the handoff.

I'm going back over this because my last reply put only a short recap in the next-step box and never listed the findings. The handoff names the right files and functions, and I confirmed each one in the code. What's missing is five product decisions. Without them, the implementer either guesses or builds a headline that is blank or out of date most of the time. Here they are, each with my recommendation.

## 1. Which chat's plan the card shows

The plan is stored once per project ([ProjectStateDocument.cpp:1140](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ProjectStateDocument.cpp:1140) reads a single `plan` object). The card's purpose title is stored per chat. If someone starts a second chat in the same project, the card would show that chat's purpose ("Quick fit check") above the first chat's strategy ("Fine layers with supports away from visible surfaces").

- **Show the project plan in every chat.** No new data, but the card can contradict itself.
- **Show it only in the chat that wrote it.** The plan needs one new field recording which chat wrote it. Plans saved before that field existed have no owner, so you'd decide whether those show everywhere or nowhere.

**My recommendation:** show it only in the chat that wrote it, and change only the card. The model can keep seeing the project-wide plan, as it does today.

## 2. What "out of date" means on the card

This is the main one. Every edit marks the plan as needing reassessment, including the agent's own edits ([ProjectPersistence.cpp:148](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ProjectPersistence.cpp:148) doesn't check who made the edit). The `plan_set` tool tells the model to call it *before* applying changes. So in the normal journey, the plan is marked stale a few seconds after it's written.

- **Hide or dim stale headlines.** In practice almost every headline gets hidden or dimmed.
- **Ignore staleness.** The card keeps vouching for the strategy after you change things by hand.
- **Decide from the change log the card already receives.** If every change since the plan was written came from the agent, show the headline normally. If you edited a setting, restored a version, or switched presets since then, show it marked as written before your edits.

**My recommendation:** the change-log rule. It reuses data the card already has, it leaves the model-facing validity flag alone, and it needs no new tracking of who wrote what. One assumption I haven't checked: that the plan's sequence number and change-log sequence numbers come from the same counter. The rule depends on comparing them. One known weakness: if the agent changes strategy without calling `plan_set` again (the October 12 vase run did this), the card shows the old headline as current. That's left to the prompt's "refresh the headline" instruction.

## 3. What the card shows when there's no headline

The model is only told to call `plan_set` before applying *several* changes. A one-setting request produces no headline. Of the three October 12 journeys, one never called it, and the other two wrote generic headlines ("Prepare X for PLA printing"). So many cards would lose their middle line.

- **Accept the gap.** The card is just shorter: purpose, presets, estimates.
- **Ask the model to call `plan_set` whenever it settles on a strategy.** More headlines, but that's a bigger prompt change and more tool calls per turn.
- **Show a placeholder** like "No plan yet."

**My recommendation:** accept the gap for now and measure how often headlines are missing in the live evaluation. Only then decide whether to change when the model calls `plan_set`.

## 4. The "N objects with overrides" note

It shares a line with "3 more changes," so the handoff's "remove the counts" sweeps it out too. It isn't a preset difference, though. It tells you some objects print with their own settings, which is easy to forget, and the headline won't mention it. `overrideObjectCount` is about three lines and only the card uses it.

**My recommendation:** keep it.

## 5. The `origin` field also reaches the model

The handoff says to remove `origin` (the agent-or-person label on each preset difference) if nothing else uses it. Something does: tool results send it to the model ([AgentHost.cpp:2798](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/AgentHost.cpp:2798)), and it appears 817 times in the recorded requests in `tests/project_prompt/requests.json`. No prompt or skill mentions it. An implementer following the handoff literally might stop at this point or keep the whole attribution system.

**My recommendation:** remove it anyway, call it out as an intentional change to what the model receives, and re-record the request fixtures.

## Also: split the work into two phases

Decision 3 depends on data the handoff only collects at the very end. I'd split the work:

1. Make the prompt more concise and run a small live evaluation.
2. Replace the card and remove the old difference code.

Your rule is that no live-model test runs without you approving a specific batch, so the handoff should name the batch, for example: four journeys (strength, appearance/supports, quick prototype, changed strategy), one model, one run each.

Two smaller corrections I'll make without asking:
- Two components are named `ChangeRows`. The one in `SetupCard.tsx` shows preset differences. The one in `components/ChangeRows.tsx` shows the chat's change log and must stay. The handoff should say which is which.
- The handoff is right that `plan_set` doesn't push fresh context to the card today. Only settings patches and intent updates do ([AgentHost.cpp:717](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/AgentHost.cpp:717)).

Which of these do you see differently? Decision 2 matters most, since it decides whether the headline is useful at all.

**The evidence: the old tool did the same.** Batch B still used `intent_update`, whose description said only "Record the user's explicit purpose as setupTitle". Seven of its twelve titles already carried settings or strategy:

**Why I think the prompting invites it:**

1. **The field's name says "setup", not "purpose".** It's called `setupTitle`, so a model reads it as "a title for the setup" and describes the setup. Field names tend to weigh more than the sentence explaining them.
2. **The title gets no limits; the headline gets several.** For the headline I wrote what to leave out (the purpose, the file name, the printer, routine steps) and a word target. For the title there's nothing like "no settings, material or printer". In practice the only rule it has is the 120-character limit.
3. **The model doesn't know what else the card shows.** Nothing tells it the presets line and the headline sit right under the title. So it packs everything into the title to make it stand on its own.

A cheaper, less capable model like DeepSeek V4 Flash probably follows names over prose more than a stronger one would. But all four points are in our wording, so that's where I'd fix it first.

- Rename `setupTitle` to `purpose`.

## Running it

By default every case runs 3 times (`RUN_BUDGET` 60 shared by the cases run,
at most 20 for one case alone); `--runs N` sets it. `--verbose` prints every
run's conversation. Usage is logged for every response on stderr and totalled
at the end.

```bash
tests/project_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py --render-only --prompt-rev 6b4b8b6188 > bodies.jsonl
```

prints every request body it would send and their sizes, and sends nothing.

All runs of all the cases run share one pool of `--jobs` workers (5 by
default, 3 for the claude-cli backend below), and each run's line gives its
wall-clock time.

## Running on the Claude subscription (`--backend claude-cli`)

`--backend claude-cli` answers every step with the locally installed Claude
Code CLI in headless mode (`claude -p`), billed to the developer's Claude
subscription instead of a per-token API key. `--judge claude-cli` moves the
judge there as well. Neither needs a key; both need the CLI logged in once
with `claude auth login`. The runner refuses to start a run the CLI would bill
to an API key (`apiKeySource` other than the login).

```bash
tests/project_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py --backend claude-cli --judge claude-cli --case advice-infill --runs 1
```

The model defaults to `claude-opus-5-5` at effort `medium`, both pinned so a
count moves only when the prompt does (`--claude-model`, `--claude-effort`,
`--claude-judge-model`). `--claude-keep DIR` keeps each run's session file,
tool list, MCP config and the CLI's event stream for reading afterwards.

### Which backend for what

- **Iterating on a prompt or skill: the subscription.** A strong model
  answering the app's real requests, with real tool calls, shows what the
  prompt itself causes: an ambiguous sentence, a rule two sections disagree
  on, a skill that invites the wrong call. It costs no API money, so it can
  be run as often as the subscription's usage limits allow. Those limits are
  shared with the developer's own Claude Code work; start with one case and
  keep `--jobs` small.
- **Before a release: a small paid run on the app's default model.** The app
  defaults to `gpt-5.4-mini` (the OpenAI provider's default in
  `ProviderProfile.hpp`), which scored about like DeepSeek V4 Flash in the
  printer suite's model table (82 and 79 of 87, `tests/printer_prompt`,
  "Which model"). A strong model
  can paper over an ambiguity a weaker one trips on, so a pass on Opus does
  not show the shipped default will pass. That run needs Kenneth's approval
  like every paid batch.
- **The baselines below** are DeepSeek V4 Flash with the OpenAI judge, except
  the subscription baseline, which is claude-cli's own. A claude-cli count is
  compared only with that one. Changing the judge changes
  what every judged case counts, so `--judge claude-cli` results start their
  own baseline, under the same "confirmed results become the baseline" rule.

### How a recorded request reaches the CLI

`claude_cli.py` turns each recorded request into a CLI run, and
`claude_mcp_stub.py` serves the tools:

- **System prompt**: the rendered prompt, as `--system-prompt`.
- **Tools**: the stub is a stdio MCP server with the case's tools (the 28 of
  `project_tools.json`, or the point's own list), with their real
  descriptions and schemas. Every call the model makes reaches the runner
  through it, and the step rules above apply unchanged: a read is answered
  with the recorded answer, a change ends the run (the runner stops the CLI;
  nothing is answered), a response of reads decides or is answered whole.
- **History**: the request's items before its last turn are written as a
  session file the CLI resumes (`--resume <file>`), so earlier messages,
  calls and results reach the model as its own turns, tool calls and tool
  results, not as a transcript. The last turn's message (the person's words,
  the `<workspace>` block, the plate's picture) goes in as one stream-json
  user message.
- **A point recorded mid-turn**, after a tool result (`after-preview`,
  `after-apply`, `after-slice`, `after-intent`, `direct-change-applied`,
  `direct-change-failed`, `first-person`, `slice-refused-by-tool`): the
  session ends on that turn's last call, marked as a deferred call. The CLI
  runs it through the stub, which returns the recorded result, and then asks
  the model.

Nothing from the developer's own Claude Code setup reaches the model: no
CLAUDE.md, auto-memory, settings, hooks, output style, skills, other MCP
servers or built-in tools, a minimal environment, and an empty temporary
working directory. `test_claude_cli.py` checks that, and the shapes above,
by running the installed CLI against a fake Messages endpoint on localhost
(no login, nothing sent; about 10 seconds). Run it after a CLI update: the
session file is the CLI's internal format, verified against 2.1.283.

What differs from the app's request, beyond the model:

- **Developer messages.** The Messages API has no developer role, so each of
  the app's developer items (its notes after a file-load report, the skills)
  is a user text block wrapped in `<developer_message>` tags. Hosts that
  drop or demote the developer role raise the same question for the API
  backend.
- **The CLI's own text.** Before the prompt, the CLI sends a billing header
  and "You are a Claude agent, built on Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK."; after
  the first message it adds a short environment note (the temporary working
  directory, platform, date and model name) and an empty system turn
  carrying the effort setting.
- **Tool names** carry the CLI's MCP prefix: the model sees
  `mcp__jusprin__settings_get`, while descriptions, which name other tools
  bare, are unchanged. The runner strips the prefix.
- **Mid-turn points**: after the deferred call's result, the CLI adds
  "Continue from where you left off." as a user message. The app's notes
  that follow the result there (the setup skill in `after-intent`, the
  slice-failed skill in `slice-refused-by-tool`) are further text blocks of
  that same tool result, since the CLI resumes no message after it.
- **Notes sent once** (a point's `once`) stay in the history after the
  first answered read; the app leaves them out of the turn's later requests.
- **Pictures** reach the model, unlike on the pinned DeepSeek hosts, so
  `model-opened-unnamed`, `model-imported-by-tool` and `model-opened-by-tool`
  can be measured here.

The usage the runner logs is the CLI's token count; on the subscription it is
not billed per token.

## Judging a prompt or skill change

What the suite is for (Kenneth, 2026-10-19): showing that a change has not
made the prompt substantially worse. At three runs a case it detects large
regressions only, not small effects. Day-to-day host noise is small next to
what it looks for: on the printer suite the same prompt scored 76, 76 and 74
of 84 on three runs.

1. After a prompt or skill change, run the "after" batch only: the checkout,
   same model, pinned hosts and judge, three runs a case. Compare it with the
   current baseline table below. There is no before run.
2. Judging the result. There are no fixed thresholds (Kenneth,

   case by case and reads every failure and unobserved run. It decides
   whether anything looks like a real regression worth investigating, and
   says why. A case with no baseline row is judged on its own expectation.
   When it is not sure, it asks Kenneth.
3. Only for a case that looks like a regression, run it again with
   `--prompt-rev <previous revision>` the same day. That tells the prompt
   apart from changed requests or a bad host day; a bad host day usually shows
   as drops in untouched cases too. A case run alone gets 20 runs, which is
   what to use before reading a smaller gap as real.
4. Baselines. The current baseline is one section. When Kenneth confirms a
   new result is good enough, it becomes the new baseline, and the old one

Merge intent_update and plan_set into one tool, setup_record

The setup card's title (what the person wants) and its headline (how the
agent will print it) were written by two tools, and the model kept them apart
badly: in batch B's changed-strategy journeys (2026-10-19) it rewrote the
headline with plan_set but never called intent_update, so the card read
"dried flowers, spiral vase" above "watertight multi-wall". The two records
were already handled as one (same coordinator block, both in-app only, both
on the chat, the same context push), so they are now one tool.

setup_record takes, all at the top level:
- purpose, required on every call, at most 60 characters: what the person
  wants the print to be or do, in a few words and their terms, not how to
  print it (no settings, material, printer or print mode unless the person
  made one of them the goal). It titles the setup card.
- fields, optional, with intent_update's semantics (assumed, question,
  provenance).
- headline, decisions, unverified, risks: the plan, optional. With a
  headline they replace the whole plan; with none the plan is kept, so a
  purpose can be recorded before there is a strategy. unverified is one
  sentence per thing taken as true without being able to check.
The result carries the intent section, purposeChange and the setup in force,
and always the plan as it now stands. The card's context is pushed once per
successful call, so title and headline arrive together.

The setup-changed skill fires on a first purpose or changed fields, as
before; a new purpose wording alone is title_only, and a call that only
restates the purpose to change the plan is unchanged, so neither fires it.

Why it looks like this (DeepSeek V4 Flash, live runs of 2026-10-19/20):
- "purpose", not "setupTitle": under either tool 7 of 12 batch-B titles,
  and some batch-C titles, described the setup ("Rhino figurine — 0.16mm,
  3 walls, organic supports"); with the rename and the description every
  title in two later batches was goal-only.
- A flat plan, not a nested object: the model sent the nested plan as a
  string of JSON, which the registry refuses; two refusals end a turn.
- "unverified", not "assumptions": next to fields' "assumed" flag, the
  model put intent-field objects under assumptions. This last rename has
  not been run live.

Changes to the model's input: one tool where there were two (27 project
tools), "purpose" and "unverified" in each turn's <workspace> block and in
tool results (including workspace_inspect's plan section), the project
prompt's line "the print's purpose recorded with setup_record, a setup that
suits it, checked, ...", and the setup-changed skill's "record the plan,
with what is unverified, using setup_record first".
